alignment.note: Greek uses future indicative with passive participle (ἔσεσθε μισούμενοι, periphrastic future passive); Vulgate employs a simple future with dative of disadvantage (eritis odio, 'you will be for hatred'); Syriac uses future with passive participle (ܬܗܘܘܢ ܣܢܝܐܝܢ), mirroring Greek structure but with different morphological realization.

Greek employs ὑπὸ πάντων (genitive plural with preposition, 'by all'); Vulgate uses simple dative omnibus without preposition; Syriac uses ܡܢ ܟܠܢܫ (preposition + collective singular 'from everyone'), a typical Semitic idiom for universal agency.

Greek uses prepositional phrase with article (διὰ τὸ ὄνομά μου, 'on account of the name of me'); Vulgate mirrors this with propter nomen meum; Syriac omits the article (ܡܛܠ ܫܡܝ), as Semitic languages typically lack the definite article before possessed nouns with pronominal suffixes.

Greek uses aorist participle ὑπομείνας (substantival, 'the one having endured'); Vulgate employs future perfect sustinuerit (relative clause construction); Syriac uses imperfect with relative particle ܕܢܣܝܒܪ ('who will endure'), shifting from completed to durative aspect.

Greek εἰς τέλος ('unto the end') and Vulgate in finem use directional prepositions; Syriac employs ܥܕܡܐ ܠܚܪܬܐ ('until the end'), using a temporal preposition with the noun for 'end/latter time', semantically equivalent but lexically distinct.

Greek uses simple future passive σωθήσεται ('will be saved'); Vulgate employs future with predicate adjective salvus erit ('will be safe/saved'); Syriac uses imperfect ܢܚܐ ('will live'), a semantic equivalent focusing on the result of salvation as life rather than the passive act of being saved.
